title: Git: first commit to GitHub
intro: From a local folder to a repo on GitHub, step by step.

blocks.p: This command turns your project folder into a Git repository. It creates a hidden .git folder where Git stores all version history. If you already did this, you can skip it.

git add moves files into Git’s “staging area” so they are ready to be committed.

. means “all files in the current directory.”

You can also add files individually: git add filename.

git commit saves a snapshot of your staged files into Git history.

-m "message" lets you attach a message describing the commit. Here "Initial commit" is a conventional message for the first commit.

blocks.h: Link your local repo to GitHub (set remote origin)
blocks.p:
git remote add adds a new remote repository.

origin is the standard name for the main remote (you can name it differently, but most people use origin).

The URL is your GitHub repo URL. Replace username and repo_name with your GitHub username and repository name.

blocks.h: Check if it was added correctly
blocks.p:
This will show something like:

origin  https://github.com/username/repo_name.git (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/username/repo_name.git (push)

git push uploads your commits to the remote repo.

-u sets origin/main as the default upstream branch, so in the future you can just run git push without specifying the branch.

origin is the remote name we just added.

main is the branch you’re pushing to. (Older repos sometimes use master; check your GitHub default branch.)

blocks.h: Pushing a new branch for the first time
blocks.p: -u sets upstream so next time you can just do git push
